title: A cosmic flame
caption: The Flame Nebula (NGC 2024), imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
credit: ESO/IDA/Danish 1.5 m/R. Gendler, J.-E. Ovaldsen, C. Thöne and C. Féron

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: On the fringe of a huge cloud of gas and dust shines the Flame Nebula, with a dark, forked structure of dust across the centre of the image. The nebula, also known as NGC 2024, lies towards the constellation of Orion.
In fact it conceals a cluster of massive, young, blue stars. Their light sets the gas ablaze, and the nebula's typical colour comes from hydrogen atoms heated by these stars.

Yet the stars themselves can't be seen here. They are hidden behind that dark, forked band of dust, and only infrared observations can reveal them, because infrared light passes through dust far more easily than visible light. This picture, made in visible light, shows the glowing gas the stars light up rather than the stars. It was built from three short exposures with the 1.5-metre Danish telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, through blue, visual and red filters.

understand.summary: The DFOSC camera on the Danish 1.54-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Even with telescope exposures, visible light can't reach the hidden stars; seeing them takes infrared, which the eye cannot detect.

explore: The exposures lasted 40 seconds in B, 80 seconds in V and 40 seconds in R. The Flame Nebula lies about 1,300 light-years away.
alt: A glowing nebula at the edge of a gas cloud, with a dark, forked dust structure in the centre.
